subtitle: Choose when, where, or how much work runs.
summary: Pip’s film must be ready by morning, but the electricity forecast changes through the night. The same computation can have different operational emissions at different times or places. Pip learns three responses: time shifting, location shifting, and demand shaping. The first two move execution; the third changes the offering. None cancels a deadline, data constraint, capacity requirement, or service promise. Book-era updates, charging, media, and hackathon examples show the transferable idea: create useful flexibility, then act on a relevant electricity signal rather than assuming night or low price means green.

concepts.title: Intensity changes with time and place
concepts.body: “The whole country is green,” says a poster. Pip needs a more precise clue: electricity carbon intensity for this region and hour, expressed as CO₂e per unit of energy. Generation and demand vary. The plant meeting extra demand may differ from the average mix, so average and marginal signals answer different questions. Pip labels the chosen signal and interval instead of treating a national reputation—or an overnight timetable—as a measurement.

steps.text: Pip asks for evidence about the actual execution interval.
Generation and demand affect electricity emissions.
Record whether the method uses an average or marginal perspective.

concepts.title: Time shifting preserves the job
concepts.body: The cinema’s opening film needs two hours to render and must be ready by 06:00. Pip reaches for “Start,” then spots a cleaner electricity forecast at 02:00. There’s time to wait—but forecasts can change. Pip keeps the same film, quality, and deadline, and sets a fallback so a disappearing clean window cannot cancel the show. This is time shifting: move the work, not the promise.

steps.text: Pip must preserve the morning screening.
The same film still needs two hours of work.
Use a deadline-preserving fallback if that window disappears.

concepts.title: Location shifting moves the execution
concepts.body: A distant region looks cleaner on Pip’s chart. Moving the export there might reduce electricity emissions, but can the data travel? Pip checks approved regions, transfer costs, capacity, availability, latency, and jurisdictional constraints before moving anything. A cleaner destination with no room for the job is not an option. Time shifting can avoid some relocation problems by keeping data and execution in place; neither route removes the service’s obligations.

steps.text: Pip considers moving execution, not just changing its label.
The candidate region has a lower electricity estimate.
Move only when the complete execution remains feasible.

concepts.title: Demand shaping changes the offering
concepts.body: The electricity signal rises while a visitor requests a preview. Pip offers a lighter version, preserving the essential result and explaining the choice. This changes the offering: demand shaping, not simply running the identical job later. Like a video call keeping audio when video quality falls, the product needs an agreed minimum. Pip must know what users require and whether they can choose the lighter mode before reducing quality.

steps.text: Pip checks what the visitor actually needs.
The electricity signal triggers an agreed response.
Keep essential functionality and explain the experience to the user.

concepts.title: Forecasts support constrained decisions
concepts.body: Pip’s forecast looks perfect; the chosen worker is unavailable. Electricity information alone cannot schedule a film. Capacity, forecast quality, workload knowledge, and service objectives all constrain the decision. If the signal disappears, Pip follows a documented fallback and records why no carbon-based choice was possible. The book’s supplier and hackathon examples belong to its publication period. Their lasting lesson is to add a carbon signal to operational decisions, not replace every other constraint.

steps.text: Pip combines the signal with workload knowledge.
A forecast can change or disappear.
The documented fallback still meets the service promise.

misconceptions.claim: Running overnight is always carbon aware.
misconceptions.correction: A fixed clock schedule does not establish cleaner electricity. Compare the actual signal for eligible execution times.

misconceptions.claim: Demand shaping means moving an unchanged job to another region.
misconceptions.correction: That is location shifting. Shaping changes the service’s resource demand or quality.

scenario.title: A render with a morning deadline
scenario.context: Pip’s film takes two hours to export and must finish by 06:00. A fictional forecast suggests cleaner electricity at 02:00, but it may change. The job must stay in its approved region. Pip can shift the full export or offer a lightweight preview now while the full result follows.

options.label: Shift the complete export within its deadline
options.benefit: Preserves output quality while using a cleaner predicted interval.
options.cost: Requires scheduling, a duration estimate, and a fallback when the forecast fails.
options.consequence: The scheduler chooses an eligible start and records the signal used. It runs before the deadline even if the cleaner window disappears.

options.label: Offer a lightweight preview now
options.benefit: Reduces immediate work while giving the user something useful.
options.cost: Changes the product experience and can add wasted work if both versions are always generated.
options.consequence: The team defines when a preview is useful and whether full output is still required. It measures combined preview and final-export work.

scenario.debrief: The first choice shifts the same job; the second shapes the offering. Both need clear user expectations and a complete accounting boundary.

quiz.question: A two-hour job must finish by 06:00. Which start is infeasible?
quiz.explanation: A 05:00 start finishes at 07:00. Carbon intensity cannot override the stated completion constraint.

quiz.question: Reducing optional video detail during high grid intensity is…
quiz.explanation: The application changes its offering and resource demand rather than merely changing execution place.

quiz.question: A region has a lower forecast intensity but lacks required capacity. What should the scheduler do?
options: Choose among feasible alternatives and preserve the service constraint
Treat the forecast as a capacity reservation
quiz.explanation: Electricity data does not guarantee compute availability. The decision must satisfy both.

exercise.title: Write a carbon-aware scheduling policy
exercise.prompt: Choose one flexible job. Define its eligible execution window, carbon signal, and fallback. If you instead shape demand, state exactly what changes for the user.
